source.title: Athlete Health and Human Performance Will Not Improve Without Transdisciplinary Collaboration and Data Sharing in Elite Sport

paper.citation: Tenan, M. S., & Alejo, B. (2024). Athlete health and human performance will not improve without transdisciplinary collaboration and data sharing in elite sport. Journal of Athletic Training, 59(10), 979–983. https://doi.org/10.4085/1062-6050-0580.23
paper.abstract: How can elite-sport organizations move beyond medical and performance silos toward shared evidence generation? Editorial argument; no participant sample or evaluated implementation. Collegiate and professional sport organizations. Organizational recommendations are conceptually relevant to Baylor but require local governance, authority, and workflow design. Narrative editorial contrasting medical and high-performance models and proposing a transdisciplinary information hub. Uses examples and cited literature rather than original empirical methods. Distinguishes transdisciplinary shared frameworks from interdisciplinary coordination.
paper.tldr: This editorial informs organizational design for integrating health, performance, and research data while preserving medical autonomy and privacy. The authors argue for a centralized data-broker architecture while allowing disciplines to keep separate source systems. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Narrative editorial contrasting medical and high-performance models and proposing a transdisciplinary information hub. Uses examples and cited literature rather than original empirical methods. Distinguishes transdisciplinary shared frameworks from interdisciplinary coordination.
paper.findings: The authors argue for a centralized data-broker architecture while allowing disciplines to keep separate source systems. They explicitly recommend rule-based, role-appropriate access under FERPA, HIPAA, local need-to-know rules, and contextualized dashboards rather than unrestricted sharing. They propose combining routine real-world data with specialist causal-inference expertise as an alternative evidence path when randomized trials are impractical.
paper.limitations: This is an editorial; it does not test whether the proposed structure improves athlete health, performance, workload, or staff burden. The overtraining/RED-S example is illustrative and should not be treated as a validated multi-signal detection algorithm. Centralization increases privacy, security, consent, governance, and model-misuse risks; the article notes legal consultation and formal agreements. Real-world causal inference still depends on design, data quality, confounding control, and domain/statistical expertise.
paper.practicalImplications: Build shared decision questions, data definitions, access rules, and escalation ownership before a central dashboard. Preserve independent medical authority and minimum-necessary access; use integrated data to support review and evidence generation, not to automate diagnosis or employment decisions.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Build shared decision questions, data definitions, access rules, and escalation ownership before a central dashboard. Preserve independent medical authority and minimum-necessary access; use integrated data to support review and evidence generation, not to automate diagnosis or employment decisions. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
